fields.description: Seen once in the six-machine 2400-operation stress model (step 2297, a sync on machine 1 failed with GIT_ERROR; the rerun of that sync succeeded, fsck clean, integrity 0). The preserved sync.git had 4 packs and 5 loose objects, so git's auto gc (gc.autoDetach) had repacked it in the background several times during the run; a mktree/hash-object/commit-tree racing the repack's deletion of loose objects is the probable cause (the same shape as the review's V8_PruneOnThePrivateSyncRepo, which saw 'git mktree: fatal: entry ... is unavailable'). Pre-dates the package split (no git behaviour changed). Proposed fix: bead owns sync.git, so set gc.auto=0 there and run the maintenance itself under the store lock (repack -d when loose objects pass a threshold), never detached; keep origin's receive-side gc as the remote's business. Needs a test that provokes the race.

data.text:
Audit of roll-dih8.3, 2026-10-09, main a455383050e40c75b202cd33141de6d0098461b1. Scope: inspect the feature and existing query behavior; no source edits or feature implementation.

Verdict: the P2 feature is justified and still unimplemented. The issue currently has only a one-sentence description and no acceptance criteria. The graph and existing readiness predicate already support an additive query implementation; no event-format, storage, sync or ownership-protocol change is needed.

Verified observations:
1. bead ready PARENT --json exits 2 with USAGE (unrecognized arguments). cli.py:256-258 has only --epic and the shared flags. cmd_ready at commands.py:563-571 aliases --epic to --parent, and select at :547-549 matches immediate parents only. With epic E -> nested epic N -> task T, global ready contains T but both ready --epic E and ready --parent E return []. The same omission affects ready descendants below closed or deferred intermediate parents. This is the feature gap already tracked here, not a new duplicate issue.
2. P2 validation defect: scope IDs are resolved inside the candidate loop after other filters. On an initialized empty tracker, ready --epic missing and ready --parent missing both succeed with []; on a populated tracker the former raises ISSUE_NOT_FOUND, but adding --label absent makes it succeed with [] again. A typo can therefore masquerade as an exhausted work queue. Resolve a supplied scope before filtering, even when there are no candidates. select is shared with list, so a fix there must preserve direct-parent membership.
3. API ambiguity: supplying --parent A --epic B silently ignores B (commands.py:566). In the fixture A had two ready children, only one shared with B; the command returned both. Define selector compatibility before adding a third spelling.

Proposed acceptance criteria (recommendations from this audit, not implemented):
- bead ready [PARENT] adds optional recursive scope. Without PARENT, output and behavior stay as they are. Accept any issue type as the root and the same full/prefix-omitted IDs that State.resolve accepts. A missing root always reports ISSUE_NOT_FOUND.
- Membership is the strict transitive closure of parent-child edges, excluding the root and deduplicating immutable issue UIDs. Use actual edges, not the display-key prefix (an imported ex-root.99 with no edge must stay out). Walk every parent link in multi-parent graphs and terminate on merged/imported cycles and deep chains.
- Traverse through intermediate issues regardless of status, ownership, type, label, or other output filters. In the 16-issue fixture, the recursive result should contain ex-leaf, ex-shared, ex-below-closed and ex-below-deferred. Their containing nodes need not themselves be ready.
- Readiness is the existing predicate evaluated against the full State: open, no confirmed claim, no status conflict, and no blockers. An ancestor or a second parent outside the selected subtree still contributes blockers. Do not redefine readiness as leaves only: a ready non-epic parent and its ready child can both appear. Preserve provisional-claim and disputed-status behavior.
- Apply existing user filters and deterministic ordering (priority, created_at, id), then the limit. Keep the ready JSON array/text output and read-only/no-network behavior. --limit 0 remains unlimited.
- Recommended compatibility choice: keep existing --parent and --epic as direct-child selectors; make the new positional form recursive. Explain the distinction in help/prime and README. Reject simultaneous scope selectors instead of silently discarding one. If --epic is to become recursive, that needs an explicit documented compatibility decision rather than an incidental change to select.

Implementation boundaries: add the positional parser argument in cli.py; put an iterative descendant query in queries.py using State.children (model.py:362-369); filter membership in cmd_ready while using the full state for readiness. Do not reuse reaches/waits_for: waits_for also follows blocking dependencies and would put out-of-scope prerequisites in the subtree. The descendant query may later serve roll-dih8.4, but this feature does not depend on recursive close. Record the final semantics in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 and README; add behavioral regressions and a FINDINGS row for the validation defect when fixed.

Regression coverage to add during implementation: nested epics and non-epic parents; full and prefix-omitted root IDs; valid leaf root; absent root with empty/filtered-out candidates; multiple parents and diamond deduplication; cycles including the root and a chain beyond the recursion limit; closed/deferred/claimed intermediates; external ancestor blockers; status conflicts and claims; filters/order/limit after scope; misleading dotted IDs; legacy selectors and conflicting selectors; JSON/text and unchanged exports.

Validation completed in this audit:
- 6 existing focused tests passed: BpTest.test_readiness_follows_the_rule_br_uses; ReplayAuditBugs.test_second_parent_blockers_hold_child; ReplayAuditProperties.test_tombstoned_blocker_unblocks_unless_status_disputed; ReplayReaudit.test_merged_parent_cycle_matches_br_readiness; Review5CLI.test_e11_parent_filter_matches_every_direct_parent; Review6.test_prime_matches_ready_and_help_outside_a_repository_is_silent.
- 12 synthetic CLI probes in a Sandbox with its own BEAD_HOME, repository and local bare remote reproduced the cases above. Imports were offline; exports before/after query probes were identical. An initial scratch assertion expected VALIDATION for the positional parser failure; the observed code was USAGE, the assertion was corrected, and the complete probe run passed.
- Full baseline/stress not rerun for this source-unchanged, scope-limited audit. The prior implementation/validation session is recorded on roll-dih8.8/.9. Working tree remains clean.

Minimal reproductions (run only in a scratch repository with a scratch BEAD_HOME): init --prefix ex --offline; create E -t epic --offline; create N -t epic --parent E_ID --offline; create T --parent N_ID --offline. Then compare ready --json (contains T) with ready --epic E_ID --json ([]), and ready E_ID --json (USAGE). On that populated tracker compare ready --epic missing --json (ISSUE_NOT_FOUND) with ready --epic missing --label absent --json ([]).

Audit complete. The implementation remains open; release the audit claim so the work can be picked up with these findings. P2 priority remains appropriate.

Decision, 2026-10-09, from the maintainer (asked in this session, with br 0.5.7's behaviour as evidence): bead ready --epic ID becomes recursive like br's (br documents --epic as 'sugar for --parent <id> --recursive, depth-unbounded and cycle-safe' and refuses --epic with --parent). The new positional bead ready ID means the same: ready issues anywhere beneath ID. --parent ID stays direct children only, as in br's ready --parent and bead's list --parent. No -r/--recursive flag. This overrides the audit's recommendation to keep --epic direct-only. Probed in a scratch repo: br ready --epic E excludes the root (also when the root sits in a parent cycle), walks through closed and deferred intermediates and every parent link, keeps second-parent blockers from outside the subtree, accepts a prefix-omitted root, returns [] for a leaf root, and reports ISSUE_NOT_FOUND for a missing one; bead's global ready matched br's on the same fixture.

data.reason: Done in e9ec582 on main (committed locally, not yet pushed). bead ready ID and bead ready --epic ID (as in br) are ID's subtree: every issue beneath it through parent-child edges, at any depth and through every parent link, whatever lies in between; the root is excluded; parent loops and a 1,100-level chain terminate. Readiness is judged on the whole tracker. --parent stays direct children, in ready and list. Audit defects fixed: a scope is resolved before filtering (ISSUE_NOT_FOUND, list --parent too), and ID/--epic/--parent are mutually exclusive, each given once (USAGE). Docs: README, REVIEWING.md section 2 (the --epic decision), FINDINGS J01-J03, CHANGELOG. 1. Run a read-only differential on a copy of the real store: show, list, ready, export, info, log and claims under a scratch BEAD_HOME. Never a write: the copy routes to the real remote.
2. Before the gate or launcher removal, give every retained infrastructure driver explicit executable selection, including infra/drive.py, infra/roundtrip.py and infra/compat_real.py. The local override is BEAD_UNDER_TEST as an absolute path; drive.py also accepts per-host absolute executable overrides, with the installed path retained as its default. Helper discovery stays anchored to the source tree. Run this rehearsal with staged Rust binaries and throwaway stores before replacing live installations; step 7 governs that later replacement. soak.py already takes the binary as its first argument; its caller passes the selected Rust path. Preflight must record the selected executable path and version on every participating machine and verify the expected Rust build. Run drive.py and soak.py with Rust on all four machines and only the provided throwaway repository's test refs.
3. Update the documentation of §8: README, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, REVIEWING.md, FINDINGS.md, MIGRATING.md, CHANGELOG.md.
4. Tag the last Python commit python-0.1.0.
5. Remove the Python package, tests/, pyproject.toml, ./bead and the Python CI.
6. Set version 0.2.0.
7. Upgrade every development machine from source. Quiesce bead processes and keep writers stopped through replacement. Enumerate every workspace sharing the installed executable, sync each remote-backed workspace with the old binary and require no pending ownership or unpublished work; inspect local-only workspaces without attempting to sync them. Verify the old Python runtime uses its default 4,300-digit integer limit, resolving compatibility first if it does not. Keep a store copy and the previous Python install revision; run the read-only comparison on copies of all affected workspaces. Then install from source with the checkout or git command in §8, using --root ~/.local so the executable replaces ~/.local/bin/bead. Preserve accepted .command receipts: sync does not remove them, and the Rust and rollback Python binaries must recognise them. Record the installed path and version, verify bead info for every workspace (integrity [] and pending_ownership []), and only then resume writers. If verification fails, leave writers paused, reinstall the saved Python revision, and recheck every workspace before resuming. Keep the current store and receipts; do not restore an old snapshot over newer accepted work. Same-store rollback compatibility is proven by .12.
8. After ./bead is removed, preflight the retained drivers again and prove they still launch the explicit installed Rust binary.

So one tracker splits by locale (and, in a mixed fleet, by implementation). Found 2026-10-10 in a python:3.14-trixie container with the locale generated: test_hardening.G13_TrackedConfigIsUtf8WhateverTheLocale.test_latin1_claim_excludes_a_utf8_claim errors against Python's ./bead (the harness cannot decode the Latin-1 ref from git for-each-ref) and passes against the Rust binary; a direct probe (init under LC_ALL=en_US.ISO-8859-1, then git for-each-ref | od -c) shows the two refs. macOS is unaffected (Python's filesystem encoding is always UTF-8 there), and CI's Linux runners skip the test when the locale is not installed. Rust's behaviour is the one G13 intends; Python should hand git the ref's UTF-8 bytes whatever the locale.
fields.title: Under a Latin-1 locale on Linux, Python's bead names the coordination ref in Latin-1 bytes

fields.description: Python starts git through subprocess with close_fds=True (beadroll/base.py, run_git), so git gets only stdin, stdout and stderr; the Rust runner (crates/beadroll-git/src/runner.rs: Command::new("git") with a pre_exec that only calls setsid and resets SIGXFSZ) passes on every descriptor bead inherited without close-on-exec. Found 2026-10-10 while porting test_commands (roll-k2wy.7): with a git shim on PATH that logs ls /dev/fd, sh -c 'exec 7</dev/null; exec BEAD create probe --json' shows git seeing 0 1 2 3 4 under Python's ./bead and 0 1 2 3 4 7 under the Rust binary (3 and 4 are the shim's own). A pipe the caller waits on (a harness's output, a make jobserver) can then stay open after bead exits, held by git; it may also be why nextest flags Rust runs 'leaky' more often. Python's behaviour is the contract: a git child must not inherit descriptors beyond 0-2, for example by marking every inherited descriptor close-on-exec at start-up in beadroll::sys, or by closing them in the runner's pre_exec, with a test that fails without it.

Appendix A of docs/RUST-PORT.md budgets the replay of 200,000 events at 150 MB. Measured in roll-k2wy.13 (2026-10-10, this Mac, `cargo run --release --package xtask -- timing --replay 200000 [--ownership]`), a fresh process that loads the journal from disk and replays it peaks at 921 MB, and at 958 MB when about half the events are ownership events in attempt files. The loaded journal alone peaks at 670 MB and 747 MB.

Where it goes:
- Every event is kept as its parsed JSON object (`Value`) beside its typed operation. That is about 2 KB an event: each object is an `IndexMap` with a `String` per key, and an event makes about 27 allocations.
- Replay's own share is 210-250 MB, mostly registers (`BTreeMap<EventId, Value>`, a leaf of about 1 KB each) and dependency tags as `Issue` holds them.

Both are public types of beadroll-core: `Value`/`Object`, `Event::value()`, `Issue::registers()`. The CLI and xtask use them. Meeting the budget needs:
- a compact event representation that builds values on demand, or at least shares keys;
- smaller register and tag containers.

That is an API change across crates, outside Phase 4's scope.

For scale, Python peaks at 722 MB and 1.70 GB on the same histories, and the largest real tracker has 280 issues.

fields.description:
Found in roll-k2wy.13 (2026-10-10). Every bead process of a store fetches outside the store lock (Python's synchronise, beadroll/sync.py:584; the Rust port does the same), into a ref of its own, refs/beads/fetch/<pid>-<hex>, and deletes that ref after the fetch. A fetch's connectivity check runs `rev-list --not --all` in sync.git. git lists the loose refs before it reads them, takes a ref deleted in between for a broken one and, with ref paranoia on by default, dies on it: `fatal: bad object refs/beads/fetch/<other pid>`. The concurrent command then fails with REMOTE_UNREACHABLE although the remote answered. A rarer second form is `cannot lock ref ... unable to create directory`, when a deletion removes the empty directory another process is creating its ref in. This is G16's scenario (agents in several worktrees sharing one store), which its tests reach only by chance.

Both implementations have the race. Measured with plain git, seven processes fetching at once and then keeping their refs:
- Python's sequence (`update-ref refs/beads/remote TIP`, then `update-ref -d <fetch ref>`, each a call of its own): 0 failed fetches of 7,000.
- One `update-ref --stdin` transaction started before the fetch (Phase 4's first build): 13 of 2,100.
- Pure ref churn with no fetch at all: 564 of 14,589 `rev-list --all` runs died the same way.

Python's calls take long enough for the other fetches' checks to be over first; they do not remove the race. roll-k2wy.13 went back to Python's two calls: G16's Rust test, four copies at once, failed 8 of 120 runs with the transaction and 0 of 120 after. Python's G16 test against that binary, eight copies at once at load 20-25, failed 2 of 200 (0 of 200 with the binary from before Phase 4): too few to separate, but not zero, and Phase 4 makes processes reach their fetches closer together.

Ways out, both behaviour changes for after the cutover (docs/RUST-PORT.md §1):
- `transfer.hideRefs=refs/beads/fetch` in SYNC_REPO_CONFIG: fetch's connectivity check runs `rev-list --exclude-hidden=fetch` in git 2.55, so it would not list other processes' fetch refs; check git 2.40, the oldest supported. This removes only the bad-object form.
- Retry a fetch that fails on another process's fetch ref, or on creating its own: this covers both forms.

Once it is fixed, the two update-refs after a fetch can become one transaction of the link's long-lived update-ref again, which saves 8-10 ms of a sync and of a publishing write (docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A).
fields.acceptance_criteria: Many bead processes syncing and claiming at once on one store (G16's shape, repeated under load) never fail on another process's fetch ref: no 'bad object refs/beads/fetch/' and no 'unable to create directory', under git 2.40 and the newest git. The change is recorded in REVIEWING.md and CHANGELOG.md.
fields.title: Concurrent fetches on one store can fail: git dies on another process's fetch ref, deleted while it lists refs

data.text:
git budgets, measured 2026-10-10 on this Mac. These are release builds of main (95baf22) and of the consolidation, run interleaved one by one in a scratch tracker of 30 issues on a local bare remote. Each figure is the median of 15 runs, measured twice. git processes were counted by a logging git first on PATH. The machine was under load, about 5, and main ran about a fifth slower than in a first measurement on a quiet machine. docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A has the table and the explanation.

- Reads (budget about 15 ms): met. show, list and ready take 15.4-15.6 ms, against 20.6-21.2 ms for main in the same run, and info takes 15.2-15.4 ms against 24.5-24.9 ms. They start 3 gits (info: 4 before). On the quiet machine the same 3 gits took 12.6-13.1 ms.
- A publishing write against a local remote (budget about 90 ms): missed. create and comments add take 126.6-127.1 ms against 207.6-210.5 ms for main, and claim takes 123.7-127.1 ms against 204.8-213.4 ms. They start 14 gits instead of 26-27. A sync with nothing new takes 62.5-63.1 ms against 129.8-131.7 ms, with 10 gits instead of 20. Why the budget is missed:
  - The first build met it on the quiet machine: 91-94 ms with 10 gits, and a sync in 42 ms with 8.
  - That build asked HEAD and the transport settings when the workspace was found, before the store lock, while Python asks them after it. It also set the fetch refs in one transaction.
  - Making the Rust bead ask and write as Python does, where Python does, put four gits back:
    - a rev-parse of HEAD and its branch each time a transaction starts, about 4 ms;
    - the transport settings' config each time a link is made, 4-6 ms;
    - Python's two update-ref calls after each fetch instead of one transaction, 8-10 ms. As a transaction, they deleted the fetch ref while concurrent fetches on the same store were still listing refs, and git failed those (G16). Python has the same race; it is filed as roll-dih8.12, and fixing it would allow the transaction again.
  - Of what is left, the push takes about 35 ms (most of it the remote's receive-pack), the fetch about 15 ms, and each other git about 4 ms, a millisecond of that the runner's fork. The audited setsid needs pre_exec, which rules out posix_spawn.
  - Writing objects in-process would save hash-object, mktree and commit-tree, under 10 ms now that the first two start while the round reads. That is not justified (docs/RUST-PORT.md §2.3d).
- Replay (budget 0.5 s and 150 MB for 200,000 events): the time is met and the memory missed, as the comment of 15:44 explains (roll-dih8.11).
- The fast suite (docs/RUST-PORT.md §4.7, target at most 2 minutes on this Mac): missed. After Phase 4, the suite's 676 tests took 195 s on the Rust binary and 216 s with Python's launcher as the bead under test (643 tests in 211 s at Phase 3's close). The load was about 14 during that run, from Spotlight's indexing and another project's process. §4.7 records it. The commit is e12a76a.

For step 3 (documentation, §8), from roll-k2wy.13 (2026-10-10): these lines describe Python's replay and are wrong for the Rust bead, whose ancestry index is a chain decomposition (docs/RUST-PORT.md §2.3c), not one bitset per event, and whose replay takes 0.26 s for 200,000 events. They are README.md 399-401 (Known limits: one bitset per event, about 60 MB at 10,000 ownership events, 'a permanent implementation would use a reachability index'); docs/REVIEWING.md 86 ('No persisted projection (replay is ~80 ms)'), 87-88 (the same bitset limit) and 257-258 (reviewers are asked to attack State.saw's version vectors 'and bitsets for ownership events'). Rewrite them for the chain clocks (each event's furthest position on each chain; saw is clock[chain] >= position), with Appendix A's numbers.

A clue from roll-k2wy.13 (2026-10-11): under git 2.40.4 (built from source in the Debian trixie container), the new test children::a_sync_git_whose_config_lost_its_format_version_is_made_again passed against both binaries. It makes its SHA-256 project with git init --object-format=sha256 and a SHA-256 bare origin, never a clone, and bead's sync pushes refs/beads/journal from a SHA-256 sync.git to that origin over the local transport. So git 2.40 can push SHA-256 repositories there. G26's setup differs: it clones the still-empty SHA-256 origin and pushes from the clone. A likely cause, not yet checked, is that git 2.40's clone of an empty SHA-256 repository is made in SHA-1, and that is what the receiving end refuses ('does not support this repository's hash algorithm'). If so, the test could commit in a checkout made with git init --object-format=sha256 and push from there, and run under 2.40 like the rest.

Root cause (2026-10-11): not a protocol defect; the test's fault injection races the remote's own git maintenance. After every push the sandbox remote's receive-pack starts 'git maintenance run --auto' detached (receive.autogc defaults to true; in git 2.55 the default strategy outside scheduled maintenance is geometric). Its loose-object estimate samples objects/17 alone and multiplies by 256, so two of the remote's ~28 objects landing there (about 1 run in 200) read as 512, over maintenance.geometric-repack.auto=100, and the remote repacks itself in the background: one pack of every object, a cruft pack, a multi-pack-index, the loose copies pruned. Shown on a scratch remote of 4 loose objects, 2 of them in objects/17: one plain push left no loose object. In the test, if the repack finishes before the test looks, the tip is not loose (line 54 fails; seen once in ~780 runs at load ~160); if its pack is written but the loose copies not yet pruned when the test deletes the loose tip, the commit survives in the pack, b's fetch gets it, and b's claim rightly succeeds on a commit the remote still has (seen once in ~2,135 runs with diagnostics: after the deletion, git cat-file -t on the remote still answered commit, from a pack written 2 s before b's claim holding all 25 objects, two of them 17...). When the commit is really gone, the fetch fails ('not our ref'), so b cannot claim on it. Fix: the sandbox's bare remotes get receive.autogc=false, so a remote changes only when a test changes it, with a test that pushes into a sandbox remote whose objects/17 holds two loose objects (maintenance in the foreground) and checks the pushed commit stays loose. To land after roll-k2wy.16.

Fix prepared on branch k2wy20-autogc (a3ecbd2, on top of the cutover's removal, to land after roll-k2wy.16): every bare repository a test sandbox makes has receive.autogc false. A new test, sandbox::tests::a_push_leaves_the_remotes_objects_as_they_arrived, writes two loose objects into objects/17 of the sandbox remote, runs its maintenance in the foreground, pushes, and finds the pushed commit still loose: without the fix the push returns with the remote repacked (pack, cruft pack, multi-pack-index), with it nothing is packed. The pruned-remote recovery test with the fix: 2,000 runs, 48 at once, load ~250, no failure (before it: 2 in ~2,900, one of each symptom).
